title: I Built the Missing Guardrails Package for Dart
summary:
I shipped a Flutter app to production last year with an LLM chatbot baked in. Two weeks later a user pasted their Aadhaar number into the chat, the model echoed it back, and I spent a weekend writing a PII scrubber by hand. That scrubber grew into ai_guardrails.

Python has NeMo Guardrails, Guardrails AI, LLM Guard. Dart had nothing. If you're building AI features in Flutter or server-side Dart, you've been on your own for input/output safety. This package closes that gap: 35 scanners, 893 tests, zero runtime dependencies, runs anywhere Dart runs.

What it actually does

ai_guardrails sits between your user's text and your LLM call. Input scanners run first: they can redact PII, block prompt injection attempts, catch leaked secrets. Then your LLM runs. title: Tailwind CSS Alternatives: When UnoCSS or Panda CSS Makes Sense
summary:
Tailwind CSS became the default utility-first framework for React projects in 2023-2025. By 2026, alternatives have matured enough to deserve serious consideration. UnoCSS brings dramatic performance improvements and unmatched flexibility. Panda CSS offers type-safe, CSS-in-JS-style ergonomics without the runtime cost. Plain CSS with custom properties handles simpler projects without framework overhead. Here's the practical decision guide.

Quick Answer

Tailwind CSS is the right default — mature tooling, extensive community, and excellent documentation make it the safe choice for most projects. UnoCSS is the choice for performance-critical applications, complex design systems, and projects where Atomic CSS's generated class explosion is a concern. Panda CSS is the choice for teams wanting typed, component-oriented styling without Tailwind's utility syntax. summary:
Building an Incident Response Agent That Remembers with Hindsight

Introduction

In software development, production incidents are unavoidable. A server may suddenly become unavailable, a database connection may fail, an API may stop responding, or an application may experience unexpected performance issues.

When these problems occur, DevOps engineers must identify the cause, investigate logs, find a solution, and restore the service as quickly as possible.

However, there is one important problem: teams often solve similar incidents repeatedly because the knowledge gained from previous incidents is not always available when a new problem occurs.

What if an AI agent could remember previous incidents, understand how they were resolved, and use that experience to help engineers handle similar problems faster?

title: The Cleanup Script Was Right About the Name and Wrong About the File: Dynamic Includes and Leftover-File Hunts
summary:
Every few weeks we run a maintenance pass over the servers we look after. One step is a hunt for leftover files in web roots: the fix_something.php, test2.php, debug_login.php and install.php files that pile up on any server that has been alive long enough. They are worth hunting. On one pass we found a debug script that printed a payment provider's API credentials to anyone who opened it, an installer that still created an admin/admin123 account, and a "test" file that dumped server details.

So the hunt is useful. It is also how we broke a live product page on a customer site, and the way it happened is worth writing down, because the check we relied on looked solid and was not.

title: Agent Distraction
summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases
